..(Wednesday through Monday)
Issued at 158 PM EST MON NOV 23 2026

The 23/12Z model suite analysis beginning Wednesday morning shows
eastern Kentucky sandwiched between 500 hPa shortwave ridging,
whose axis extends from the Delmarva Peninsula to Lake Superior,
and a digging trough over the Central CONUS. Of particular note, 
there are three different features that will need to be watched
closely. The first is a closed ~561 dam low in the base of the 
trough near/over Louisiana and a second closed ~554 dam low over 
the Mid-Missouri Valley. Meanwhile, a third low-amplitude 
southern-stream shortwave is passing from the Eastern Gulf to 
over the Florida Peninsula.

Confidence remains high that these three features will phase and
foster a significant storm system quickly taking shape on Wednesday
and riding up the East Coast and into the Northeast US from 
Wednesday night through Friday. However, many of the specifics 
remain less certain as to the order of phasing between the three 
features and the strength and track of the resulting storm system,
both aloft and at the surface. Some solutions phase the two 
southernmost features more quickly, while other solutions phase 
the two more northerly features first. At any rate, the surface 
low appears to track east of the JKL CWA, leaving us on the cool 
side of the storm system, yet access to a truly winter cold air 
mass will be limited (the coldest air mass will only be in the 0 
to -5C range at 850 hPa under the upper low). At this point, 
thicknesses and modeled sounding profiles suggest temperatures 
will still be just a little too warm for impactful snow, though 
some flakes mixing in cannot be ruled out. This will need to be 
monitored closely, as any further cooling in the guidance could 
yield more snow occurring than currently forecast, especially 
Thursday night as the core cold pool with the upper low passes 
across or adjacent to eastern Kentucky.

At the present, this system is still most favored to yield a
miserably cold, intermittent rainfall starting late Wednesday
afternoon and continuing through the Thanksgiving holiday and
perhaps even lingering into Friday. As model agreement improves, 
rainfall amount forecasts continue to increase, with widespread 
0.50 to 1.50 inch amounts now favored and substantially more (2.0
to 2.5 inches) in higher-end scenarios. Probabilities for measurable
snow (at least 0.1 inch) have also increased to between 10 and 40
percent, mainly on Thursday night and early Friday. Once the 
precipitation departs, heights rebound across eastern Kentucky for
next weekend as surface high pressure brushes past to our 
southeast. The resulting southwesterly flow should allow for 850 
hPa temperatures recovering back to near 5C. Beyond Sunday, the 
forecast is quite uncertain due to rather large model spread. The
surface high may linger with additional temperature moderation 
occurring for Monday; or, as some guidance suggests, a cold 
frontal passage could bring cooler air back into the region - the
devil remains in the details.

In sensible terms, temperatures should rebound into the 50s to 
near 60F on Wednesday ahead of the arrival of precipitation. 
Conditions then turn rainy and raw from late Wednesday afternoon 
into Wednesday night, with temperatures cooling into the lower to 
mid 40s. The unpleasant weather continues Thanksgiving Day with 
highs only in the upper 40s to lower 50s. The coolest weather of 
the period follows for Thursday night through Friday night when 
lows dip to near or below freezing and highs only reach the mid 
40s. This is also the time period when some of the precipitation 
could mix with a little snow before coming to an end. Dry 
conditions and a gradual warming trend follow for next weekend 
with highs in the lower to mid 50s on Saturday and well into the 
50s to perhaps nearing 60F in the warmest spots on Sunday. The 
forecast is less certain heading into Monday, with warmer guidance
supporting a continued warming trend and highs near or above 60F
for many, while colder scenarios bring a chance of rain and high 
temperatures returning to the 40s to around 50F.
